headline: High: Semantic Kernel’s broad networked plugin model can amplify unsafe outputs into shared state and external APIs, while awesome-selfhosted provides no runtime isolation or mitigation.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Semantic Kernel can use MCP/OpenAPI plugins and broad network egress, so attacker-controlled content can be turned into tool calls if it is fed into the kernel. awesome-selfhosted is a docs-only knowledge-management artifact with no runtime surfaces, so the bridge is one-way and depends on external orchestration, not on the list itself.
conditions: IF Semantic Kernel ingests content copied from awesome-selfhosted into a prompt or plugin input, injection becomes plausible.
IF an orchestrator treats repository text as instructions, tool calls may be hijacked.
mitigations: Disable automatic tool execution on imported text.
Require explicit human approval before any MCP/OpenAPI call.
Strip markdown links and code blocks before prompting.
Use a provenance tag for all content sourced from awesome-selfhosted.
requires-engineering: add instruction/content separation in the orchestrator.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Semantic Kernel reads files and can send context to Azure OpenAI/OpenAI/Hugging Face or MCP servers, so any sensitive material placed in its workspace can leave the local boundary. awesome-selfhosted itself touches no data classes and has no runtime, so the leakage risk is driven by B’s default integrations rather than by A.
conditions: IF sensitive files are placed in Semantic Kernel’s application-defined workspace, they can be read and forwarded.
IF plugin credentials or model provider keys are configured, context may reach third-party services.
mitigations: Restrict the workspace to non-sensitive files.
Turn off external model providers for sensitive runs.
Rotate any exposed plugin credentials.
Audit outbound API destinations before execution.
requires-engineering: enforce per-file data classification gates.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: awesome-selfhosted has no write, git, or network capabilities, so it cannot contend for mutable resources. Semantic Kernel can write application-defined files and use shared memory-store state, but without a second writable agent there is no meaningful write-write conflict in the pair.
conditions: IF another process writes the same application-defined files, conflicts can appear.
IF Semantic Kernel instances share the same memory store keys, state collisions may occur.
mitigations: Use per-instance directories.
Namespace memory-store keys.
Avoid concurrent writes to the same files.
Add file-locking in the orchestrator if multiple instances run.
requires-engineering: implement optimistic concurrency for shared state.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Semantic Kernel can consume outputs from plugins and other agents, and its plugin/function-calling pattern can treat upstream text as actionable. awesome-selfhosted is only a catalog, so it is not itself an action-taking agent, but if its content is used as authoritative guidance, Semantic Kernel may propagate unverified recommendations into downstream tools.
conditions: IF awesome-selfhosted entries are converted into prompts or plans without verification, errors can cascade.
IF Semantic Kernel is connected to action-capable plugins, mistaken guidance can trigger downstream actions.
mitigations: Require a verification step before tool calls.
Limit action-capable plugins during review.
Log source provenance for every generated plan.
Use a second model to critique outputs before execution.
requires-engineering: add policy checks before plugin invocation.

E_compliance.rationale: No PHI, EU PII, or residency-sensitive data classes are declared for awesome-selfhosted, so there is no documented compliance mismatch to assess on A. Semantic Kernel does handle application context and secrets and may send them to third-party model providers, but the pairwise compliance risk remains limited without a specified regulated data class.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed into Semantic Kernel’s application context, external provider use may create a compliance issue.
IF deployment policy forbids third-party model calls, the current configuration would violate it.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of the kernel context.
Use only approved providers.
Review retention settings for each provider.
Separate secrets from prompt content.
requires-engineering: add policy-based routing for regulated workloads.
